Olipop, the US gut health soda brand, has unveiled a leadership change as it prepares for its next stage of its growth.

The functional beverage brand revealed that Christian Patiño Webb will take over as chief executive officer.

Founder, Ben Goodwin, will step into the role of Executive Chairman and Head of Innovation at the beverage brand.

The brand was founded by Goodwin in 2018 with the mission to reshape the US soda addiction with a healthier alternative.

It has been featured in the Times100s Most Influential Companies in 2024 and it is now in one in five households in the US.

In a Linkedin announcement the company said that Olipop continues to grow in "scale, complexity, and reach" with the appointment of Webb, who has previously worked at Unilever and most recently for Electrolit, the hydration beverage brand, as CEO "marking an important moment in this evolution."

He will oversee business operations, distribution, organisational execution, brand expansion, and strategic growth initiatives.

Goodwin will continue to shape the long-term vision of the company by driving breakthrough innovation.

"Working in close partnership, Ben will help guide business strategy, ensuring the company continues to build on the vision that created the functional soda category, while Christian brings the leadership expertise needed to expand its impact on consumers," the statement said.

Goodwin said on Linkedin that he wants to focus his energy where he has the most passion and can contribute "most meaningfully."

He described the move of bringing in a CEO as "adding horsepower rather than simply reallocating focus."

He added: "Given all that, I decided it was time to explore bringing in a new CEO - someone who could be a powerhouse operator and help drive the business in a mission-aligned way, while allowing me to double down on innovation, research, culture, marketing, thought leadership, and strategy."

Webb also commenting on Linkedin said: "What Ben Goodwin and the entire Olipop PBC team have built is extremely special. They created a category that has changed the way people think about soda while staying deeply committed to their mission, their consumers, and the values that have guided the company from the beginning.

"My focus will be on scaling the business for the future, investing in our people and capabilities, strengthening execution, and building on the strong foundation already in place. Most importantly, I'll be listening, learning, and working alongside this exceptional team as we continue to expand OLIPOP's impact on consumer health at scale."

Olipop taps Electrolit head as next CEO.

Founder Ben Goodwin will move into a more innovation-focused role at the prebiotic soda brand while Christian Patiño Webb takes the top executive spot.

Published Aug. 12, 2026

Dive brief:

* Olipop has appointed Electolit chief executive Christian Patiño Webb as its next CEO as the prebiotic soda brand looks to expand growth after passing the half billion-dollar sales mark last year.
* Patiño Webb will take the top position later this month, with current CEO and founder Ben Goodwin set to step into a research and strategy focused role, according to a LinkedIn post Tuesday.
* Webb will be tasked with charting the new phase of growth for Olipop to "help drive the business in a mission-aligned way" as Goodwin hopes to "double down" on areas like innovation, he said in the LinkedIn post.

Dive insight:

Olipop's leadership transition comes as it faces increased competition in the better-for-you soda market. As more consumers seek out functional attributes from their beverages, industry stalwarts such as Coca-Cola and PepsiCo are upping their functional offerings to keep up with new market entrants like Olipop and Poppi.

Last year, Olipop reached a $1.85 billion valuation following a funding round led by Growth Equity Partners. The company has also deliberately upped its research in gut health to back up its health claims and stand out against mounting competition.

"As OLIPOP has surpassed the half-billion mark and professionalized, I've been reflecting on where I can have the greatest impact going forward," Goodwin said in the post. "I want to focus my energy where I have the most passion and can contribute most meaningfully, while bringing in a counterweight to strengthen the areas I'm stepping away from - adding horsepower rather than simply reallocating focus."

As the soda brand gears up for the next phase of growth, it is hiring an executive with years of CPG experience.

Prior to Electrolit, Patiño Webb worked at Unilever as the vice president of marketing for SmartyPants Vitamins, according to his LinkedIn. He also previously worked at Day One, a sparkling water and CBD company.

In his own LinkedIn post, Patiño Webb said he would focus on scaling the business for the future, strengthening execution and building on the company's foundation.

"The opportunity to help scale that impact while preserving what makes OLIPOP PBC special is what made this role so compelling to me," Patiño Webb said.

attributes.body:
Olipop prepares for growth with new CEO.

08.12.2026

OAKLAND, CALIF. - Functional soda company Olipop has named Christian Patiño Webb as its new chief executive officer to support its next stage of growth.

Patiño Webb succeeds Ben Goodwin, founder and CEO, who is transitioning to executive chairman and head of innovation for the company.

Goodwin, who founded the company in 2018 to support digestive health, will focus on the company's long-term vision, advance innovation and also shape its next phase of growth while also stewarding its mission, values and culture and will work in partnership with Patiño Webb.

Patiño Webb comes to Olipop from Electrolit, where he most recently was CEO.

During his career, Patiño Webb also has worked for Procter & Gamble, Johnson & Johnson, Red Bull and Unilever.

"Founding and leading Olipop to mainstream success has been the honor of my lifetime, and I feel extremely fortunate and proud of what we've accomplished to date," Goodwin said. "The team and I spent significant time carefully selecting a CEO and Christian unequivocally rose to the top. His clear track record of scaling consumer brands that have a focus on product quality and are driven by a strong founder vision make him a fantastic fit for the next leg of our journey. In addition to that, his character is exactly what we look for in an Olipop leader - strong principles and humility combined with a robust competitive hunger."

Olipop has been scaling its functional soda - formulated with a blend of plant fiber, prebiotics and botanicals - in recent years.

The company closed on a $50 million Series C funding round that gave the business a valuation of $1.85 billion last year, and previously raised $30 million in a Series B funding round in 2022.

Starbucks ranks #3 in Best Beverage Marketing Campaigns 2026.

Starbucks ranks #3 in The 25 Best Beverage Marketing Campaigns of 2026: What Actually Worked, an index that ranks 25 beverage brands against a set of qualitative marketing effectiveness dimensions. Starbucks sits behind Liquid Death at #1 and Red Bull at #2, and ahead of Dunkin' at #4. Its position is anchored by a loyalty ecosystem the index cites as one of three models, alongside Red Bull and Prime, that set the standard for cultural reach and earned-media volume.

What The 25 Best Beverage Marketing Campaigns of 2026 measures.

The index presents a ranked list of 25 beverage brands assessed against a stated set of qualitative marketing effectiveness dimensions: category, primary channel, and "what worked." It also includes a separate qualitative assessment of AI and LLM discovery readiness for select brands. No numeric scoring methodology, panel, or weighting formula is described. For that reason, Starbucks carries a rank of #3 without a published numeric score.

Why Starbucks ranks #3.

Starbucks is categorized in Coffee, and the index identifies its primary channel as app plus loyalty plus seasonal drops. Under the "what worked" dimension, the index states that Starbucks succeeded because its marketing was embedded into daily routine.

The center of Starbucks's ranking is its loyalty ecosystem. The index cites that ecosystem as one of three models, alongside Red Bull and Prime, that set the standard for cultural reach and earned-media volume. That places Starbucks in a small group singled out for how its loyalty structure translates into cultural reach and earned coverage.

The index draws a specific distinction about how Starbucks Rewards functions. It describes Starbucks Rewards as a behavioral lock-in system, not just a loyalty program. In the index's words: "Starbucks Rewards is not a loyalty program, it is a behavioral lock-in system." That framing separates Starbucks Rewards from conventional points programs and ties it to the "what worked" finding that Starbucks embedded its marketing into daily routine.

How Starbucks's loyalty ecosystem drives its position.

The index groups Starbucks within one of its cross-brand patterns: brands that embedded into behavior, where apps, routines, and rituals created behavioral lock-in. Starbucks Rewards is named directly as an example of this pattern, alongside Keurig subscription architecture. The pattern connects back to the brand-level finding that Starbucks's marketing worked because it was embedded into daily routine, and to the index's characterization of Starbucks Rewards as a behavioral lock-in system rather than a loyalty program.

Starbucks's primary channel, described by the index as app plus loyalty plus seasonal drops, reflects the mechanics behind that behavioral lock-in. The app and loyalty components carry the routine, while seasonal drops supply recurring reasons to return.

Where Starbucks sits in the broader beverage story.

Beyond behavioral lock-in, the index calls out patterns that shaped which beverage brands performed in 2026. It notes that brands built brands, not just campaigns, with consistency across channels creating identity rather than just awareness, and that brands designed for sharing, with content distributed by users rather than only consumed. It also observes that brands moved at the speed of culture, treating timing as strategy.

The index additionally flags a divide in AI and LLM discovery: brands with structured, entity-rich content footprints are getting cited by AI engines, while brands with only paid media spend are invisible in AI answers. The index names Olipop, Athletic Brewing, and Liquid I.V. as positioned well for AI retrieval, and states that several others on the list are not, and that the gap will widen in the next 24 months. Starbucks is not named among the brands the index positions well for AI retrieval, and it is not named among those it does not.

Starbucks's #3 rank rests on a specific, repeatable mechanic: a loyalty ecosystem the index groups with Red Bull and Prime for cultural reach and earned-media volume, and a Rewards program it defines as a behavioral lock-in system. Going into the next refresh, that behavioral embedding is the position the index credits Starbucks with holding.

I tried all the flavors of Olipop prebiotic soda I could find and ranked them from worst to best.

Jun 26, 2026, 6:59 AM PT

Over the past couple of years, Olipop and other brands of prebiotic soda have surged in popularity. In 2023, Olipop was set to pass $200 million in sales and was listed as one of the 10 most popular brands among Gen Z.

The popular prebiotic soda brand claims to support digestive health through the use of prebiotics, plant fiber, and botanical extracts.

At just 45 calories or less per can, I decided to find out what all the hype was about and try it for myself. I picked up 17 flavors of Olipop at my local supermarket and ranked them from worst to best.

Here's what I thought of the flavors I tasted.

Of the 17 varieties I tried, watermelon lime was the only flavor I found to be off-putting.

I was really excited about Olipop's watermelon-lime flavor - until I took my first sip. Out of the 17 flavors I tried, this was the only one I found to be truly off-putting.

In my opinion, it tasted like watermelon that had been put in the fridge after sitting out in the sun all day. This flavor also overpowered any lime notes that may have been in there.

To be honest, I disliked it so much that I wondered if maybe I had gotten a bad batch. After trying another can from a different store, I found it tasted the same as the first one.

My wife tried both cans and didn't care for it either. Maybe this flavor is more of an acquired taste.

Olipop's crisp apple tasted like a green-apple lollipop.

Anyone who chooses green apple when presented with a variety of lollipop flavors will enjoy this soda. However, I happen to dislike green-apple candy, and that's mostly what Olipop's crisp apple tasted like.

Every can of Olipop has a description of the flavor, and this one claims to blend "sparkling apple juice and gummy apple rings." However, I tasted a lot more of the latter.

The cherry cola tasted slightly medicinal to me.

Throughout my taste test, I was surprised by how few of the sodas tasted medicinal. However, the cherry cola was an exception.

In my opinion, it had an unpleasant aftertaste and a cherry flavor that seemed more artificial than other Olipop varieties.

I expected the banana-cream flavor to be my least favorite.

I expected to rank banana cream dead last - I love bananas, but I'm not sure I've ever liked anything banana flavored. In that context, the banana cream was surprisingly drinkable.

The banana flavor was definitely more reminiscent of Runts candy than an actual banana, but it wasn't too strong or sweet.

The classic root beer didn't leave me wanting more.

Olipop's take on root beer definitely had some of the familiar, sweet, herbal taste. However, it didn't pack much of the spicy bite the best varieties offer.

In my opinion, root beer typically translates poorly into diet form - maybe because it's traditionally so sugary - and Olipop's decidedly tasted like a diet root beer. It wasn't unpleasant, but it didn't leave me wanting more.

Olipop's orange squeeze tasted like a traditional orange soda.

According to the can, Olipop's orange squeeze incorporates clementine, mandarin, and lemon juices. However, in my opinion, it tasted more like traditional orange soda.

Although this had plenty of citrus flavor, it didn't have much of the associated tartness.

I didn't think the cherry-vanilla soda had a well-balanced flavor.

The cherry taste that shined through in the cherry-vanilla soda was tart with acidity. I found it to be closer to the flavor of real, fresh cherries than maraschinos.

However, the distinct cherry flavor was a little too assertive for my tastes, and I would've liked more of the familiar warmth of vanilla to balance it out.

I thought the Olipop ginger ale had a strange aftertaste.

At first sip, I thought Olipop's ginger ale might rank first on this list. It had the flavor of real ginger - just enough to give it just a touch of spice.

It also had a nice, citrusy tartness, which made for a brighter and more nuanced flavor than you'd find in most mainstream ginger ales.

However, there was something oddly biotic about the aftertaste that brought this one down the list.

I was surprised that Olipop's Doctor Goodwin didn't taste like Dr. Pepper.

Based on the name and packaging, Doctor Goodwin is presumably Olipop's answer to Dr. Pepper. However, Olipop's version tasted nothing like it.

That said, this soda wasn't bad at all. It had a more palatable dose of the same cherry flavor from the cherry-vanilla variety. However, it was balanced out by an indistinct sweetness.

To me, Doctor Goodwin might viably pass as a cherry cola.

The vintage-cola flavor reminded me of Diet Pepsi.

At the first taste, I was impressed by how fizzy the vintage cola was. I was also surprised at how accurately it mimicked the flavor of familiar diet colas like Diet Pepsi.

It was sweet, had a touch of bite, and no noticeable aftertaste. If I lined it up with other diet colas in a blind test, I'm not sure I'd be able to tell which one had 9 grams of fiber.

Olipop's lemon-lime soda was refreshing.

Lemon lime seems pretty ho-hum as far as soda flavors go - so much so that this was the last of the 17 sodas I tried. However, I was surprised by how much I liked it.

Unlike any other lemon-lime soda I can remember, I could taste the distinct flavors of lemon and lime instead of a vague citrusy sweetness. It was pleasantly sour and very refreshing.

The strawberry-vanilla soda had a better flavor balance than the cherry-vanilla version.

Strawberry vanilla was another flavor that surprised me. Based on the cherry-vanilla variety, I thought this one would be too heavy on the strawberry flavor.

But while the sweet, tangy taste of strawberry was certainly present and obvious, this one had a much more noticeable hint of vanilla, which served as a warm counter to the strawberry.

Olipop's classic grape flavor tasted like its namesake.

Olipop's classic grape didn't taste much like a standard grape soda. Instead, I found it tasted more like actual grapes.

More specifically, it was reminiscent of the fancy sparkling grape juice that comes in glass bottles and is served to kids when the grown-ups are having cocktails. It was tart, not too sweet, and a little winey.

I liked Olipop's Ridge Rush more than Mountain Dew.

In 2024, Olipop introduced its Ridge Rush flavor with an ad campaign that called it "A Can of Do" - positioning it as the brand's answer to Mountain Dew.

However, I liked it a bit more than actual Mountain Dew - it wasn't as sweet, and the citrus flavors were far more distinct.

When I tried the tropical punch, I immediately tasted pineapple.

The biggest shock of the taste test came when I poured some tropical punch into a glass. I expected the liquid inside to be red or pink, but instead, it was yellow.

This made a lot more sense once I discovered the most noticeable flavor in the soda was pineapple. However, it wasn't nearly as thick or cloying as straight pineapple juice, and the pineapple's sweet acidity tasted brighter and lighter from the carbonation.

This felt like it was begging for some rum, though I'm not certain prebiotic rum is the best idea.

I enjoyed the spice of the ginger-lemon flavor.

The ginger lemon had even more ginger flavor than the ginger ale.

The flavor was strong enough to make the soda a bit spicy and taste like ginger beer, but it also had just enough sweetness to take the edge off the spice.

And, most importantly, it didn't have the same unpleasant aftertaste as the ginger ale. I did find that the ginger flavor overpowered the lemon, but I liked this soda so much that I was OK with it.

Olipop's cream soda was my favorite.

In general, I typically find cream sodas to be bland. However, there was nothing bland or boring about Olipop's cream soda. It was rich with vanilla flavor but not too sweet.

It was definitely on the milder side of the flavors I tried, but it absolutely captured the nostalgic soda-shop taste of cream soda.

This story was originally published in May 2024 and most recently updated on June 26, 2026.

Founder mode, tested: scope, not temperament.

Paul Graham's "Founder Mode" essay detonated in September 2024 and consumer brands have been arguing about it ever since. The thesis, born from Brian Chesky's account of nearly losing Airbnb to conventional management advice: the "hire good people and give them room" playbook fails founders, and the skip-level, detail-obsessed mode everyone calls micromanagement is, in founders' hands, the thing that actually works. Two years on Lampworkbrands has enough data - and enough wreckage - to say what founder mode means in DTC specifically: where it's the whole ballgame, where it kills companies, and what the leadership stack of a winning consumer operator actually looks like.

* The data leans founder: Bain/HBR found founder-involved companies outperformed the rest of the Fortune 500 by 3.1x over 15 years; founder-CEO firms file 31% more patents.
* Consumer's star operators are detail-tyrants where it counts: Olipop's Ben Goodwin still leads formulation at a ~$500M-revenue company; Peter Rahal personally drove David's product spec after RXBar.
* But DTC's graveyard cuts both ways: founder mode without financial discipline (Outdoor Voices) fails exactly as hard as professional management without product conviction (Peloton's revolving door).
* The resolution: founder mode is a scope decision, not a temperament - stay in the details of taste and the model; delegate the encoded procedures completely.

What the discourse got right.

Chesky's core observation survives contact with consumer: at brand companies, the product is the founder's judgment, serialized. Graham's "skip-level" instinct is just proximity to truth - the founder tasting the formulation, reading raw support tickets, watching the creative tests. Goodwin at Olipop is the cleanest case: CEO of a company that crossed $400M revenue in 2024, valued at $1.85B, still personally leading product formulation - "keeping us really locked on target for the vision" in his words. Rahal ran the same play twice: RXBar to a $600M Kellogg exit with ~75 employees, then David from launch (Sept 2024) to a reported ~$140M first year - both built on a founder who refused to delegate the core spec. And the Bain numbers say this isn't survivorship poetry: insurgent mission, frontline obsession, owner's mindset - measured, they outperform.

What the discourse got wrong.

Founder mode became a permission slip, and the failure cases were predictable. Outdoor Voices is the canon: Ty Haney's product instinct built a genuinely loved brand, but founder mode extended into unit economics and board management, the company burned to a $40M valuation from $110M, and the "adult supervision" that followed didn't save it either - stores closed abruptly in 2024. Peloton ran the inverse experiment: push out the founder, install a decorated professional CEO (Barry McCarthy, ex-Spotify/Netflix), and watch him exit in two years alongside 15% layoffs - three permanent CEOs in three years. Away cycled founder out, in, and out again. The pattern across the wreckage isn't "founders good" or "managers good." It's that swapping the person is a category error when the missing thing is a system. Charity Majors' critique of the essay - that it rebrands micromanagement and builds dependency - is right precisely for companies that never encoded how they operate.

Founder mode is a scope decision. Stay unreasonably close to taste and the model. Delegate everything you can write down - by writing it down.

The synthesis: founder mode on top of a standard.

Here's the version I'd defend with its own money. The founder's non-delegable scope is narrow and absolute: product taste, brand meaning, the economic model, the bar for people. Everything else - service workflows, media operations, reporting, reconciliation - gets encoded (its LSOPs) and run by a small senior team with agents underneath. This is also, quietly, what the best operators already do: Beckham writes essays about empowering people while personally holding Simple Modern's mission and margin logic; Frank calls himself a "fireman CEO" - in the details wherever there's a fire, out of them where the system runs. Chesky himself converged here, telling Decoder that in the AI era "you need to be founder mode, because you're going to need to move like a startup" - speed of adaptation, not span of control, is the point. Founder mode without a standard is heroism, and heroism doesn't scale. A standard without founder mode is administration, and administration doesn't win. The stack is both.

| Decision domain | Mode | Why |
| Product spec & taste | Founder, always | The product is judgment serialized |
| Brand meaning & voice | Founder, always | Coherence cannot be delegated |
| Economic model & capital | Founder + scorecard | Ownership psychology with guardrails |
| Growth/service/ops execution | System (LSOPs + pod) | Encoded, measured, transferable |
| Hiring bar | Founder sets, system filters | Standards decay without an owner |

What this means for LAMPWORK

* When Lampworkbrands acquire, Lampworkbrands is explicitly buying the founder's judgment scope - and Lampworkbrands structure earnouts to keep taste in the building while LOS absorbs the rest.
* Its brand operators run founder-mode scope by design: full P&L, full product authority, weekly scorecard accountability.
* The diligence question Lampworkbrands always ask: if this founder leaves, what was written down? The answer prices the deal.

Own a brand this applies to?

Lampworkbrands talk to founders at every stage - long before they're ready to sell.

OLIPOP, Space Camp Wellness collab on soda-inspired lip balms.

May 20, 2026

Beauty brand Space Camp Wellness recently collaborated with OLIPOP for a set of four soda-inspired lip balms: Cream Soda, Vintage Cola, Shirley Temple and Crisp Apple.

The partnership brings together flavor, function and clean beauty, bridging the gap between what consumers sip and what they swipe, the company says.

"This collaboration brings OLIPOP's fun soda flavors into the most essential part of our beauty routines: lip balm," said Tara Piper, senior vice president of marketing at OLIPOP, in a statement. "We love partnering with Space Camp Wellness because of our shared obsession with high-quality ingredients and pure nostalgia. A lot of us at OLIPOP are nostalgic for the iconic lip balm soda collabs from when we were kids, and Space Camp is the perfect partner to reimagine the outdated version with the new twist of beloved OLIPOP flavors, like Vintage Cola and Shirley Temple."

A Space Camp spokesperson added: "From the beginning, we wanted the packaging to feel like opening your favorite can of OLIPOP. OLIPOP already has such an iconic visual identity, so our goal was to blend that with the world of Space Camp Wellness. This collaboration felt very natural creatively because both brands are rooted in everyday rituals. OLIPOP is the drink you reach for, and Space Camp Wellness is the lip balm you carry everywhere. The packaging became the bridge between those two worlds."

The lip balms, which launched May 14, are available on Space Camp's website and in-store at Target.

Full Summary

Olipop has introduced two new summer sodas - Raspberry Sherbet (a limited-edition) and Blackberry Vanilla (now a permanent flavor) - both featuring 2-5 g of sugar and 6 g of fiber per can, and is celebrating with a Berry Sipport Center giveaway for fans to win cases of the drinks.

Olipop, the social media darling redefining soda with high fiber, low sugar and real functional benefits, is officially kicking off summer with the launch of two new berry-forward flavors: Raspberry Sherbet and Blackberry Vanilla.

Inspired by nostalgic summer treats but crafted for modern wellness routines, both flavors deliver the classic soda experience with just 2-5 grams of sugar per can and digestive health support - no compromise required.

Available at retailers nationwide including Target, Walmart and Whole Foods, the new flavors arrive just in time to become your go-to sip of the season.

Olipop Raspberry Sherbet: A creamy, tangy summer scoop - no spoon required.

Raspberry Sherbet blends bright, tangy raspberry juice with smooth vanilla creaminess for an ice-cream-inspired soda that tastes like pure summer nostalgia.

Olipop Raspberry Sherbet

Inspired by classic summer scoops, Raspberry Sherbet blends tangy raspberry juice with smooth, creamy vanilla flavor for a bold, refreshing soda that tastes like pure nostalgia - no spoon required.

Part of Olipop's 6g fiber line, this limited-edition flavor delivers all the fun of a frozen treat with functional benefits to support digestive health and just 2-5 grams of sugar per can. Bright, playful and made for sunny sipping. Buy Olipop Raspberry Sherbet

* Available for a limited time
* Part of Olipop's 6g Fiber Line
* Sold in 12-ounce classic cans and variety packs
* Rolling out at major retailers and online

Is Raspberry Sherbet a limited-edition flavor?

Yes. Raspberry Sherbet is available for a limited time as part of Olipop's 6g Fiber Line. It's playful, bold, and made for fans who want dessert vibes without the sugar crash.

"Summer is the perfect moment to push our flavor creativity even further," said Tara Piper, SVP of Marketing at Olipop. "With Raspberry Sherbet and Blackberry Vanilla, we're giving fans two distinct, craveable takes on requested summer flavors - inviting them to discover their go-to sip of the season, all while supporting digestive health."

Olipop Blackberry Vanilla: the fan-favorite flavor that's finally here to stay.

After becoming one of Olipop's most-requested limited editions, Blackberry Vanilla is officially back - and this time, it's permanent.

Olipop Blackberry Vanilla

Back by overwhelming demand, Blackberry Vanilla is officially a permanent part of the Olipop lineup. This layered flavor blends juicy blackberry with crisp apple and bright mandarin and lemon juices, finished with smooth vanilla notes for a rich yet refreshing soda experience.

Crafted to satisfy sweet cravings while supporting digestive health, Blackberry Vanilla delivers classic soda vibes with modern functionality - and just 2-5 grams of sugar per can. Buy Olipop Blackberry Vanilla

This layered flavor combines:

* Juicy blackberry
* Crisp apple
* Bright mandarin and lemon
* Finished with smooth vanilla notes

Why did Blackberry Vanilla return?

Blackberry Vanilla was one of Olipop's most-requested limited editions and is now back permanently due to overwhelming fan demand. The result is a rich yet refreshing soda that satisfies sweet cravings while staying light, functional, and fridge-worthy all year long.

Introducing the Berry Sipport Center: because your Olipop deserves backup.

To celebrate the launch, Olipop is putting fans first with a clever, community-driven activation: The Berry Sipport Center.

The Berry Sipport Center is Olipop's fan-first giveaway that offers early access and a chance to win a full case of the newest flavors. Built for those all-too-relatable moments when your Olipop gets "borrowed," disappears from the fridge, or gets finished a little too quickly, the Berry Sipport Center gives fans a chance to recover lost cans - or restock early.

How does the Berry Sipport Center work?

* Fans submit a short request form explaining their "sip emergency"
* Requests are reviewed by Olipop's official Berry Specialists
* Approved entries are eligible to receive one full case of Olipop

More than 1,000 cases will be distributed during the two-week activation.

Gruns and Olipop team up on limited-edition Strawberry Vanilla Greens Gummies.

April 22, 2026

The two brands bring one of Olipop's most recognizable flavors into a functional gummy, marking Gruns' first CPG collaboration.

Gruns is partnering with Olipop on a limited-edition release that blends functional nutrition with a familiar soda profile, as the greens brand continues to expand its presence in the broader wellness category. The Strawberry Vanilla Superfoods Greens Gummies reimagine one of Olipop's best-selling flavors in a new format designed for both kids and adults, extending the reach of both brands beyond their core products.

The gummies combine strawberry, vanilla and a hint of lemon, translating Olipop's signature taste into a daily greens supplement. The collaboration reflects a broader shift across wellness, where brands are moving toward more accessible and appealing formats that fit easily into everyday routines.

For Gruns, the partnership comes at a pivotal moment. Unilever recently acquired the company for reportedly over $1 billion, signaling growing interest from major consumer players in the next generation of functional nutrition brands. The Olipop collaboration offers an early look at how Gruns may continue to evolve post-acquisition, leaning into partnerships to broaden its consumer base.

Shop the limited-edition drop through May 21 on Gruns' website.
